title: Fire Ants in a Central Texas Yard: What to Do Next
description: Found ant mounds in your Buda or Kyle yard? Learn what to record, why identification matters and what to ask before arranging a fire-ant control estimate.
summary: A practical checklist for ant mounds near patios, play areas and lawns, plus the questions to ask when comparing treatment plans.
quick_answer: Keep people and pets away from active mounds, record where activity occurs, and have the ant identified. A treatment plan should address the colony and the area at risk, not just the visible mound.
body_html:
Finding ant mounds in a Buda or Kyle backyard raises two different questions: what are they, and how should the yard be used until the problem is assessed? Start by keeping people and pets away from active mounds. Do not disturb a mound to test whether the ants are fire ants. A photo taken without approaching the colony and a description of the location can help you begin the conversation with a technician.

Make a simple record of the problem

Mark the affected spots on a sketch of the property. Note whether they are beside a patio, play area, sidewalk, vegetable garden or seldom-used corner. Include where ants have appeared indoors, if that is happening too. These details help distinguish a yard issue from a separate trail into the kitchen.

For a home in Buda or Kyle, describe the spaces your household needs to use most. This makes the estimate discussion more useful than simply reporting the number of mounds. Photos from different days can also show whether the pattern is changing.

Why the visible mound is only part of the discussion

Texas A&M AgriLife describes a two-step approach that combines broadcast bait with treatment of problem mounds when appropriate. Bait effectiveness depends on ants collecting it; moisture, product condition and application conditions matter. An individual-mound approach may suit some situations instead. Follow the product label or have a licensed professional select the method for the site. See AgriLife's fire-ant management guidance.

What to ask before scheduling treatment

  • Which ant has been identified, and what evidence supports that identification?
  • Does the estimate cover the affected spots, the lawn, or both?
  • What preparation is needed around pets, toys, garden beds and outdoor furniture?
  • What instructions apply to irrigation and access after treatment?
  • When should the result be assessed, and what follow-up is included?

Ask for the scope in writing. The right questions make it easier to compare estimates even when companies propose different approaches. Do not assume that every visit covers the same lawn area or follow-up period.

Keep the plan connected to the rest of the yard

If brown patches are also appearing, mention them separately rather than assuming the ants caused the turf damage. Excel has a lawn-pest service for assessment of listed turf pests. Ant control and diagnosis of damaged grass may involve different work.

Use the Central Texas prevention calendar to record recurring yard checks. For a quote, describe the activity through the ant-control service page or request an ant-control estimate. Excel's team can discuss the property and explain the next step.

faqs.q: Does every ant mound mean fire ants?
faqs.a: No. Identify the ant before choosing treatment. Photograph from a safe distance and describe the mound and location rather than disturbing it.

faqs.q: Can I get a fixed price from the number of mounds?
faqs.a: The number is useful, but the area, access, ant identified and proposed treatment also affect the scope. Request a property-specific estimate.
